American Samoa

American Samoa comprises five islands, representing a total reef area of 59.2 km², with 75% of tiers containing data. This case study focuses on islands belonging to the single ecoregion that encompasses the entire country (Figure 1) and its islands (Figure 2).

Coral cover observations were extracted from the ReefCloud database on 15 March 2026. A total of 507 transects from 507 sites collected between 2015 and 2023 by the NOAA’s U.S. Pacific Islands National Coral Reef Monitoring Program (Table 1) at depths varying 3 and 10 metres. At the data-tier level, observed coral cover varied from 0.5% to 69.6% with a median coral cover values estimated at 25.3% between 2015 to 2023 (Figure 3).

The extracted disturbance values indicated multiple potential events, including five years with non-zero Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) and two years with detected exposure to cyclonic waves (Figure 4). Disturbance events were infrequently captured in the data tiers: only the 2015 heat-stress event was recorded at higher intensity, and Cyclone Gita (2018) at a comparable intensity to the regional signal.

Association with Disturbances

In American Samoa, cyclone exposure was significantly negatively associated with regional coral cover, with 95% prediction intervals not overlapping zero (Figure 10). The absolute decline between the minimum and maximum observed cyclone exposure, corresponds to a 16.1% reduction in coral cover (95% prediction interval: −27.8% to -1.2%, Figure 11).

Spatially, increasing magnitude of cyclone exposure alone (i.e., excluding heat stress) contributed to regional declines in coral cover (Figure 12), with absolute losses estimated to range from 4.1% to 27.0%, and a regional average decline of 15.8% (Figure 13).
